title: Policies
text:
Use of AI
Some use of generative AI is permitted in this class, with several important constraints. (Please note that I often use generative AI myself, personally and professionally. See here for a summary of how I used Chat GPT as I developed materials for this course.)

For ALL work in this course, presenting AI-generated work (including text and ideas) as your own constitutes a violation of academic integrity. Any use of AI must be acknowledged and cited with in-text citations as shown here and/or through an AI use statement like the one that I’ll ask for as part of your final project.
In general it is fine to use basic copy-editing/spell-checking tools like the ones provided by Grammarly, Microsoft Word, and Google Docs. You do not need to include an AI use statement.
Exams: The use of AI tools during exams is not permitted and will be considered a violation of academic integrity. (Exams will be pen and paper anyway.)
Group projects: Your group will decide on your own AI use policy (see here. Any use of AI must be consistent with your group’s written policy. If any group members use AI in a way that is not consistent with your policy, that will be considered a violation of academic integrity for whoever is responsible, or for the whole group if individual responsibility cannot be determined.
Readings: I strongly discourage you from using AI to summarize the readings. The whole point of asking you to read scientific articles is so that you learn to understand and evaluate evidence for yourself, instead of taking someone else’s word for it.

title: Course Requirements
text:
Preparation
You will pretty much always need to do something to prepare for class. Usually, this is a reading, though I’ll also occasionally ask you to listen to an episode of The Language Neuroscience Podcast or watch a video.
There will be two types of readings. The specific readings are listed on that unit’s page on the course site (see Schedule).

Background readings: I’ll assign chapters from the Brennan text, encyclopedia articles, or similar sources to provide general background on a topic. Some of the material in these readings will be reinforced in class, but all of the material is fair game for the exams.
Scientific articles: We’ll also read some primary literature (real scientific papers). These will be dense and technical. It is very important to review these papers before class; otherwise, you will struggle to contribute to your group’s in-class work. But don’t worry if (when) there are parts you don’t understand. We will work through the papers together in class.

Hard copies of the articles will be handed out in class. You may reference these hard copies, along with any notes you’ve written on them, during in-class exams.






TipTips for reading scientific papers



When reviewing the scientific articles, I strongly recommend following the process here: Guide to reading scientific papers. We’ll go over this in class.

title: Course Requirements
text:
Attendance & participation
We will take formal attendance. Multiple unexcused absences will affect your individual participation grade and also your individual grade for your small group’s in-class work during that unit, see below.
During class, I’ll occasionally ask you to respond to questions in real time using a polling tool like Mentimeter. Your answers to these questions will not be graded for correctness, but repeated failure to participate in the polls will affect your participation grade.

title: Course Requirements
text:
Exams
There will be four in-person exams (including the final), each worth roughly 12% of your grade. Exam dates and grade percentages are tentative. If one exam ends up covering a longer span of the course than others, grade weighting will be adjusted accordingly. I will tell you ahead of time about any changes.
Tentative exam dates for each unit are listed on the corresponding unit page (see schedule). The exact timing of the exams may be adjusted depending on course needs. The fourth exam will take place on the date that the Registrar has set for our class.
During exams, you are allowed to reference the printed copies of any primary sources (scientific articles)1 that we covered during that unit, including any notes you have written on those copies. You are also allowed to reference a printed summary sheet.






NoteWhat’s on the exams?



The exams are designed to measure your progress towards the specific learning goals that are listed on each unit’s page. In general, they are meant to assess your knowledge of foundational concepts, your ability to evaluate and interpret scientific evidence about language and the brain. They will cover lecture material, background readings, and the primay literature that we worked through in class.

title: Course Requirements
text:
Group work on scientific papers
A significant portion of class will be dedicated to small group work.
Sometimes, you will work together to practice applying concepts from the readings/lectures. Other times, you will work with your group members to understand and interpret evidence from the scientific papers on the reading list. For example, you may be asked to create a visual aid showing how a study worked, or to use a brain atlas to visualize which brain regions were active during a particular experiment.
Some of the work will be graded as complete/incomplete. Other work will be graded on a standard letter grade scale. I’ll try to let you know ahead of time how grading will work for a particular activity, but if it’s not clear, just ask.
For each of the four main course units (see schedule), you’ll be in a different group. At the end of that unit the group will receive a grade for their work during that unit. Each of your small group grades is worth 4% of your course grade (4% x 4 units = 16% total).
Everyone in the group gets the same grade, unless there are consistent issues with an individual member’s contributions. Examples of issues that would affect an individual member’s grade include unexcused absences, failure to prepare for group work by doing the readings, or lack of engagement in the group’s discussion. If there is an issue with any student’s contributions, please let us know as soon as possible so that we can help address it.

title: LING-2801: Neuroscience of Language
text:
Course Description
This is an introductory course on language and the brain, designed for students with no background in neuroscience. Its goal is to introduce students to the major scientific findings in this area as well as the scientific process that generated this evidence. Topics include the brain regions and networks involved in language processing in the healthy brain; how these structures develop in children; and how language skills are affected by damage to these structures.

title: LING-2801: Neuroscience of Language
text:
Science for All
This course fulfills Georgetown’s Science for All core requirement. I designed the course around the learning goals of that program. According to the Science for All website:

The primary goal of courses specifically designed to fulfill the core science requirement will not be to provide a summary of current knowledge in a particular discipline, but instead to illustrate, in the context of a scientific discipline, how scientific understanding is developed, tested, and revised.

In this course, you will learn about language in the brain by studying the scientific research that led to our current understanding of this topic. There will be some traditional lectures, in which I provide conceptual background or historical context for a topic. But we will also spend a substantial amount of time unpacking and understanding specific studies. You’ll also watch demonstrations of specific research methodologies, practice evaluating and interpreting scientific evidence, and interview some of the scientists who conduct research on the neuroscience of language at Georgetown.
A secondary goal of the SFA program is this:

In addition, Science For All courses will help and encourage students to understand better the significant role that science plays in their daily lives, and will include examples of the use of scientific methods in addressing complex social problems and of the ethical issues that science can raise.

Throughout the course we’ll consider issues within the neuroscience of language that have broad social relevance. We’ll start by discussing the core scientific principle of functional localization—the idea that specific cognitive functions, like language, are handled by particular specific brain regions—along with the problematic and unscientific ways in which this idea has been interpreted throughout history. Other important topics will include signed languages and their neural representation; language networks in language-deprived individuals (i.e., profoundly Deaf people who had no access to a signed language until after childhood); and the neural and cognitive characteristics of language networks in multilingual people.

title: LING-2801: Neuroscience of Language
text:
Learning Goals
The course is designed to achieve the following overall learning outcomes:

Knowledge of the basic principles, foundational evidence, and current research challenges in the field of language and the brain

Understanding of the scientific process through which researchers learn about this field

The ability to understand and interpret scientific evidence about language in the brain

The ability to construct clear, coherent, and evidence-based scientific explanations about language in the brain
An understanding of how research on language and the brain relates to broader societal issues

Unit-specific learning goals are listed on their respective pages; see schedule.

text:
Controversies to study
Here are four major controversies in the field of language neuroscience right now. You may study any of these controversies, or an additional controversy approved by me (HRG). If you would like to study a controversy other than the ones listed below, please email me ASAP. I will need to confirm that (i) it’s a real controversy (as opposed to an issue on which the science is not controversial, even if public opinion hasn’t caught up) and (ii) there exists enough relevant and accessible literature to allow you to do the project.

Is the language network dedicated exclusively to language?
Does multilingualism protect the brain?
Are there any similarities between human brains and large language models like ChatGPT?
What is the “language network” like in infants who haven’t yet learned a language?

text:
Sources
You will identify two secondary sources relevant to your topic. At least one of these sources must be published in a peer-reviewed journal (e.g., review article, opinion piece). The other does not have to be peer review, but must be approved by me (HRG) (e.g., an episode of The Language Neuroscience Podcast).
Based on your secondary sources, you will identify the most important evidence on this topic, and the primary sources that report this evidence. You will then read the primary sources in order to evaluate the evidence for yourselves. All group members should read the paper independently and use Hypothes.is to annotate the paper and ask questions. If you still have questions after meeting in-person to try to figure it out, you may set up an appointment with me (ideally, all group members are present for this). Together, you will fill out a summary sheet to submit to me.
All references must be formatted in APA style.

title: Policies
text:
Use of Generative AI
Some use of generative AI is permitted in this class, with several important constraints.






WarningAll use of AI must be acknowledged.



In this course, presenting as your own any work that was generated with the help of AI (including text, ideas, and diagrams) constitutes a violation of academic integrity. Any use of AI must be acknowledged and cited as shown here and/or through an AI use statement like the one that I’ll ask for as part of your final project.
See here for my own acknowledgment of how I used ChatGPT as I developed this website and the course. I have not found generative AI useful for scholarly work in general, and I absolutely never use it for writing or summarizing articles (in part because I am much better at these things than AI, though I believe there are integrity and ethical reasons to avoid using AI for this as well). But I do find it helpful for technical tasks (like setting up this website) and for identifying teaching resources.


Here are some additional rules for this class:

You may NOT use generative AI to write. It is ok to make limited use of classic copy-editing/spell-checking tools like the ones provided by Google Docs and Microsoft Word, but you may not use AI to re-phrase your writing or to generate completely new text.
You may NOT use generative AI on exams. Exams will be pen and paper anyway.
I strongly discourage you from using AI to summarize the readings. The whole point of asking you to read scientific articles is so that you learn to understand and evaluate evidence for yourself, instead of taking someone else’s word for it. (Also, in my experience, genAI summaries of academic articles are often wildly inaccurate.)
For your group project, your group will decide on your own AI use policy (see here). Any use of AI must be consistent with your group’s written policy. If any group members use AI in a way that is not consistent with your policy, that will be considered a violation of academic integrity.
